entities.summary:
Pedro Nuño Colón de Portugal, 6th Duke of Veragua, played a pivotal role in the governance of New Spain, succeeding as viceroy from December 3, 1673, to December 8, 1673.

As a member of the Spanish nobility, Colón de Portugal rose to prominence through his inheritance of the titles of Veragua, Jamaica, and Gelves, solidifying his position as a key figure in the Spanish-American colonial hierarchy.

His tenure as viceroy was marked by a series of events that would shape the future of New Spain, including the attempted assassination of the Spanish viceroy, Tomás de Gálvez y Madrid, and the subsequent rebellion led by the indigenous peoples of the region.

Despite the challenges he faced, Colón de Portugal left a lasting legacy in the region, including the establishment of the Veragua title as a seat of power for the Spanish monarch in the Americas.

This fleeting yet significant period in New Spain's history serves as a testament to the complex web of power dynamics and cultural exchange that defined the Spanish colonial era.

The viceroy's own life was cut short, but his impact on the region would be felt for generations to come, as the seeds of resistance and rebellion were sown in the fertile soil of Veragua.

In the annals of history, Pedro Nuño Colón de Portugal's tenure as viceroy of New Spain stands as a poignant reminder of the delicate balance between colonial power and indigenous resistance, a balance that would continue to shape the course of American history.
